opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think representation is really the crux of it. When you look at an ARC task as raw pixels, a grid of colored cells, the transformation can look enormously complicated. Describe the same task in terms of objects, their shapes, colors, positions, symmetries, and how they relate to each other, and often the rule becomes almost trivially short. So a lot of the difficulty isn't the reasoning itself. It's finding the vocabulary in which the reasoning is simple.

That's why I'm drawn to program synthesis framings. A program is a representation, and the language you write it in determines what's easy and what's hard to express. If your domain-specific language has primitives for "find connected components," "reflect across an axis," or "recolor by some property," then a whole family of tasks collapses into short programs you can actually search for. If you only have pixel-level operations, the search space explodes and you don't generalize from three or four examples.

The interesting question is where those representations come from. Hand-engineering a DSL for ARC works up to a point, but you end up encoding your own guesses about what the task designers had in mind, and you hit a ceiling. What I find more exciting is learning the representation: systems that solve some problems, notice recurring structure in their solutions, and compress it into new reusable abstractions, so the library grows over time. That's the spirit behind things like DreamCoder: a wake-sleep loop where you alternate between solving problems and refactoring what you've learned into a better language.

Neural networks come in as the other half. Raw neural models are good at perceptual intuition, glancing at a grid and getting a sense of what's going on, but they're often brittle when you need exact, compositional generalization. Symbolic programs are the opposite. So a rich representation, to me, is a hybrid: neural networks guide the search and propose likely abstractions, while the actual hypothesis is something structured and checkable, like code. Recent work, including some of ours, has found that language models writing Python can do surprisingly well, partly because Python plus a model's prior knowledge is itself a very rich representation, much richer than a tiny hand-built DSL.

And I'd add that humans don't solve ARC from a blank slate. We bring core knowledge: objectness, counting, geometry, a sense of goals and agents. Part of improving these systems is either building in those priors or finding training regimes where they emerge. Get the representation right and learning from a few examples stops looking like magic. It starts looking like inference in the right hypothesis space.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think this is actually the central question for ARC, and it's one I've changed my mind about over the years.

When we first started working on these problems with program synthesis, the dominant approach was: you hand-design a domain-specific language with primitives like "rotate," "flood fill," "count objects," and then you search over programs in that language that map the input grids to the output grids. And that works to a point. But what you quickly discover is that the DSL is doing an enormous amount of the work. If a task needs a concept that isn't in your DSL, you're dead. And if your DSL is huge, your search space explodes and you can't find anything. So the representation isn't just one ingredient, it's basically the whole game.

The thing that I think people sometimes miss is that ARC is not really about grids. The grids are the surface. When a human looks at an ARC task, they don't see pixels, they see objects, they see a thing being pulled toward another thing, they see a pattern being completed, they see "the big one is the parent and the little ones are its children." They see something closer to a little physical or social scene. So a richer representation means moving the level of description up, away from cells with colors, toward objects with relations, intentions almost. Once you have that, the program that explains the transformation is often one or two lines. The complexity gets absorbed into the perception.

The second part, and this is where I think the field is heading, is that the representation shouldn't be fixed. It should be learned, and ideally it should be learned from the tasks themselves. This is what we were trying to get at with DreamCoder, where the system grows its own library of concepts over time. You solve some easy tasks, you notice there's a recurring chunk of program, you compress that into a new primitive, and now the harder tasks become shorter to express. The representation and the search co-evolve. I think that's a much closer picture of what human learning looks like than either "here's a giant hand-crafted DSL" or "here's a transformer, throw a million examples at it."

And then there's the obvious thing, which is that large language models have turned out to be surprisingly good sources of priors for this. They've read every tutorial and every bit of code that touches symmetry, tiling, gravity, whatever. So one way to think about richer representations now is: let the neural network propose the vocabulary and the hypotheses, and let a symbolic layer do the verification and the composition. The neural side gives you breadth and flexibility, the symbolic side gives you the thing ARC really demands, which is getting it exactly right on a novel case with three examples.

What I don't think works is pure end-to-end pattern matching on pixels, because the entire design of ARC is adversarial to that. Chollet built it so that each task is its own little universe. So if your representation doesn't let you form an abstraction that generalizes from three examples, no amount of scale fixes that. The richness has to be in the concepts, not in the pixels.

astra-6.text:
I think a lot of the challenge in ARC is figuring out what the right representation is in the first place. You’re given a grid of colored pixels, but the rule might be about objects, or boundaries, or containment, or a repeated pattern. If your system only represents individual cells, then a transformation that’s conceptually very simple can require a very complicated program.

For example, suppose the rule is to move a small object inside a larger enclosure. Once you have representations of objects and containment, that’s a fairly short description. But you still have to discover that those are the relevant concepts, and decide what counts as an object in this particular task.

So I’d want a system that can entertain multiple interpretations of the grid and search for a program jointly with those interpretations. The representation helps you find the program, and the program helps you decide whether the representation was useful.

The catch is that adding more concepts also creates more possibilities to search through. So richer representations need to come with a learned sense of which abstractions to try. Ideally, solving one problem gives you a reusable abstraction that makes the next problem easier.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the representation determines which regularities are easy to see. If you represent an ARC task as a matrix of colored pixels, then a transformation like “move this object until it touches that object” has to be expressed through lots of low-level operations. If you have objects, spatial relations, and operations like translation or reflection, that same transformation can become a very short program.

But the challenge is that there isn’t one object representation that’s right for every task. Sometimes a connected region is an object; sometimes you need to group disconnected pixels by color or recognize a shape despite missing pieces. So I’d want a system that can entertain different representations and search jointly over how to describe the input and what program transforms it.

That also creates an opportunity for learning: if you repeatedly discover useful pieces of programs, you can turn them into reusable abstractions. Then future problems become easier to express and search for. The important thing is that those abstractions have to earn their keep by helping explain new examples, rather than just giving you a more elaborate vocabulary.
